summary: An industry experience paper that catalogues five MCP server patterns (Resource Gateway, Tool Orchestrator, Stateful Session Server, Proxy Aggregator, Domain-Specific Adapter) and four anti-patterns. The catalogue comes from 15 servers: 5 from the authors' voice-AI platform and 10 reference servers. Three measurements support it: two Claude models classify 54 held-out servers (κ=0.76), a loopback transport latency benchmark, and observational production telemetry. The telemetry shows tool-selection accuracy for Claude Haiku 4.5 falling below 90% between 10 and 15 tools in context, and for Sonnet 4 between 20 and 30.

claims.claim: Tool-selection accuracy drops below 90% between 10 and 15 tools per context for Claude Haiku 4.5, and between 20 and 30 for Sonnet 4
claims.evidence: §VI-C, Fig. 2: retrospective ANSYR production logs, N=200 turns per bucket, ground truth from human post-call review. Haiku 91% at 10 vs 87% at 15 with Wilson CIs of ±4 pp, so the two buckets overlap and the 'cliff' location is not statistically resolved. The model per turn was set by tenant config, so tool count, model and tenant/task are confounded. Raw logs are not released, only per-bucket aggregates.

claims.claim: Selection accuracy declines as the number of tools in context grows, with a later onset for the stronger model
claims.evidence: §VI-C: monotone decline over buckets 1-50 for both models; direction agrees with the cited Gan & Sun (>90% up to ~30 tools) and Kate et al. Descriptive and observational; no controlled manipulation of tool count.

claims.claim: Transport overhead is dominated by network RTT, not protocol: stdio 0.01 ms, loopback streamable-http 0.39 ms p50
claims.evidence: Table III: two measured rows (N=100 echo calls). The three cross-host rows, including the Proxy Aggregator hop, are loopback plus an assumed RTT constant, i.e. modeled arithmetic. The authors label each row correctly.

claims.claim: The five-pattern taxonomy can be applied reliably (κ=0.76)
claims.evidence: §VI-A: two Claude models from the same vendor agree with each other at κ=0.76 [0.62, 0.88], but agree with the authors' labels only 68.5-75.9%. Statefulness and domain logic are systematically misread. This shows inter-LLM consistency more than taxonomy validity.

claims.claim: Four anti-patterns (God Tool, unsanitized resource content, synchronous long-running ops, vague descriptions) degrade LLM tool use
claims.evidence: §V: recorded during the authors' own development and code review and 'cross-checked' against public issues; no counts or measurement.

patterns.note: Recommends ≤~10-15 tools per context (Haiku-class), ~20 for Sonnet-class, from observational production telemetry with overlapping CIs at the threshold and tenant/model confounding.
Describes MCP server structures; does not compare MCP against other integration layers.
Sanitize backend content at the Resource Gateway; asserted, not tested.
Recommends per-tool-call logging (name, input hash, latency, size, error); no evidence.

methodology.sample: 15 derivation servers (5 own production, 10 reference); 54 held-out server descriptions; 100 echo calls per transport; 8 tool-count buckets × 200 production turns
methodology.baselines: None for patterns; tool-count is a dose-response curve without a controlled comparison
methodology.models: Claude Haiku 4.5 and Claude Sonnet 4 only
methodology.variance: Bootstrap CI on κ; Wilson CIs ±4 pp on tool-count buckets
methodology.contamination_controls: Architecture-neutral descriptions for the rater study (vs 97% on architecture-naming pilot)
methodology.languages: TypeScript/Python servers; domain is voice AI, not code

standards.peer_review: Under review (condensed version at IEEE Software); formatted for ICSME industry track
standards.artifacts: MIT replication package: corpus, kappa script, transport bench, prompts, per-bucket telemetry CSV; production logs withheld

biases.detail: Tool count and model are both set per tenant, so the tool-count curve may reflect tenant task complexity rather than catalog size.
15-server derivation corpus; ±4 pp CIs overlap across the 10 vs 15 tool buckets that define the headline threshold.
Only two Claude models, and the 'independent raters' are both Anthropic models.
Taxonomy reliability is measured between two LLMs, not human coders; agreement with authors is 69-76%.
Production session logs behind the tool-count figure are not released; only aggregates.
Table I concedes each pattern is a classical GoF/EIP pattern; the novelty is the LLM-client delta.
Transport benchmark is a JSON-RPC echo server; cross-host rows are modeled.

coi.affiliations: Carson Rodrigues: Celabe (operator of ANSYR voice AI); Oysturn Vas: University of Waterloo
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: Celabe's own production MCP servers form a third of the corpus and all of the tool-count data; Claude models evaluated
coi.detail: Explicit COI statement. The paper does not sell a product; the risk is that one company's telemetry, which outsiders cannot audit, carries the most-cited number.

verdict_reason: A candid practitioner catalogue with honest labelling of measured vs modeled rows. Its one quantitative result that matters for harness design (the 10-15 tool threshold) is observational, confounded by tenant, and not resolved at the threshold, so it is a working budget, not a measured cliff.
applicability: Directly relevant to how many MCP tools a Java team's host exposes. The defensible reading is: accuracy declines with tools in context, earlier for small models; budget ~10 for Haiku-class and ~20 for Sonnet-class, and re-measure on your own tools. Note that the paper recommends a scoped Proxy Aggregator (retrieval-over-tools) above the budget. It names the static-merge aggregator, not aggregation as such, as the failure.

conflicts_with.detail: SkillWeaver argues for per-step retrieval across thousands of tools; this paper puts the onset of degradation at 10-30 tools. They are compatible in direction but operate at different scales; neither tests the 15-100 range under control.
